column3:
I am writing to express my serious concerns about the decision to expand pétanque courts at Chimborazo Playground. This project moved forward without meaningful input from the broader community — the very residents who rely on this park every day. The land broken up for these courts was previously open green space accessible to everyone: children playing, families gathering, neighbors exercising. Redirecting that shared resource toward a niche game enjoyed by a small number of users, without a transparent public process, was an inappropriate use of city parkland and a failure of the community engagement that residents deserve.

Thank you sincerely for pausing construction and committing to a community conversation. I ask that you take the next step and permanently abandon the pétanque expansion project. Furthermore, I urge the city to restore the disturbed land to its original condition as a grassy open field — a space that belongs to all residents, not just a select few. Chimborazo Playground should serve the whole community, and I trust that you will act on that principle.

column3:
Hello Counsil Woman Newbille & Director Frelke

I believe much of the frustration surrounding the new petanque courts is the result of a communication and transparency failure from the City and Parks Department, not from the petanque community itself.

There appears to have been little visible public notice at the park, limited outreach to nearby residents, and no clearly communicated phased improvement plan showing how funding and future projects would be prioritized over time. As a result, many residents felt blindsided once construction began. I personally have lived in this area for nearly 2 years and had no idea this project was budgeted or underway. I don’t think most residents are upset that the park is being improved. I think many people are frustrated because they feel caught off guard and unclear on the broader long-term plan for the space.

I would encourage the City and Parks Department to improve public engagement moving forward by:

* posting notices and project timelines directly at the park. this in and of itself would increase visibility and transparency. 
* sharing phased multi-year improvement plans publicly, include a link to the plan on the postings in the park via QR code. 
* clearly communicating budget limitations and project sequencing
* inviting broader neighborhood input before major changes are implemented, give the people an outlet for productive discussion. 

I believe better comms and transparency would have prevented much of the current division within the neighborhood.
column4: Continue the project while Parks shares a clear phased improvement plan, project budget/timeline, and broader long-term vision for the park. Tell residents when restroom and sanitation improvements are expected, explain why the courts were prioritized first, and provide more visibility into government budget and project sequencing constraints.  From a realistic perspective, if pausing construction delays the remainder of the overall project, I would not recommend it. The core issue does not appear to be the courts themselves, but rather that residents were not adequately informed about what was happening, why decisions were made, or what future improvements are planned.

column3:
I'm a civil/environmental engineer who lives a block away. I believe there's room to expand the existing courts' capacity on the existing footprint while ALSO improving pedestrian accessibility/connectivity across the park. 

The whims of folks who already have infrastructure for their niche activity shouldn't be ignored, but this is a particularly egregious example of why public input should be highly intentional, well advertised,  and done in such a way as to not be able to be interrupted as clandestine. 

Public input aside, I'm not activist on many things but got fired up when I first saw pictures of the expansion. Why would the investment not go towards improving the sad soccer field, or some other amenity with broad appeal?

Just from a raw options standpoint, this is not fitting of a dense neighborhood in need of more turf space and play features. Since seeing it in person, I feel compelled to be more involved and happy to lend my services / thoughts if needed because multi-decade infrastructure on scarce footprints should be diversified, and barring that, at the very least the dominant feature should be able to serve more than a handful of special interest, generally-affluent people.

Thank you for taking the time to listen to the community. I am a community member who lives one block away from Chimbo playground. I am also a parent and a dog owner who uses this park every single day. It is part of our 'backyard'. Our family is biracial, multicultural and queer. This matters for reasons I will share below. 

I think a few things are really critical here: 
1. This is a historically black neighborhood. Gentrification has already pushed so many of our black and brown neighbors to the fringes of a community that has become increasingly white and class privileged. Chimbo playground area has always stood out as a more integrated space. On any given day you will see teenagers playing ball, kids of all ages in the playground, families enjoying picnics and bbqs in the grassy area and tennis courts, and members in the community garden. The Petanque courts in their former iteration, were fairly low profile and allowed for all of this beautiful diversity to co-occur. Suddenly an organization with 45 members, most of them of retirement age and white, is trying to take over this diverse space for their own interests and without input from the rest of us who use this space regularly. This is the definition of colonizer behavior and it is unacceptable. There is no world in which them hosting tournaments would make it a more diverse or welcoming space.

2. This 'back door' method of using a loophole (expansion of a current court) to get around due process and garner community feedback before ruining the park for the rest of us, has absolutely ruined all good will that we once may have had for the Petanque players. What used to be seen as a somewhat endearing group of folks playing an obscure game in the park, now is seen as a group of people trying to push the rest of us out of our own community. We will not stand for it. At this point, I propose they move the entire operation to the West End. Being part of a community means building relationships and good will, which requires transparency, authenticity and honesty. They cannot possibly come back and get the community to agree to youth leagues and tournaments after pulling this stunt. This undermines their statement about using the space to build community engagement. They simply cannot. We do not trust them.

I am only one member of a larger community, and my priorities won’t always align with those of my neighbors. I don’t expect my needs to be valued above others’ simply because they are mine. However, my concern with the petanque court expansion is less about the project itself and more about the process behind it. This situation highlights two ongoing issues with neighborhood improvements: there is no central place for community input and information, and there is no clear, transparent process for selecting or prioritizing projects. Without those structures, well‑intended efforts often fall short of their potential or serve only a small group rather than the broader community.
My family spends 4–10 hours a week at the Chimborazo Playground, yet I never saw any information about the petanque expansion—or about other recent additions, like the soccer goal, basketball hoop, or climbing structure. Some of these are wonderful (my kids love the climbing triangles!), but the hoop and goal can’t be used as intended because they were installed without any changes to the surrounding areas that would make them safe or even functional. And now the new petanque courts reduce the amount of usable space on the soccer field. I’ve heard rumors about the cost of the soccer goal—another sign that we lack a reliable, central source of information. If it did cost $4k, and if both projects were (even partially) funded or executed by DPR, the lack of coordination is concerning. Gathering community input for projects of this scale would not only increase transparency but likely lead to more thoughtful, cohesive planning.
I appreciate the CHA and the many ways they support our neighborhood. But the playground is a major community space that needs a dedicated group to help facilitate and guide projects that meet the broader needs of the people who use it (sign me up!). The Community of Chimbo organizers have already modeled how this could be done with flyers and QR‑code surveys—thank you! Overall, what’s needed is leadership and a collaborative process. It would be great if our elected councilmember could create and implement a clear structure for community participation to ensure that projects of this scale not only make sense but reflect broader community needs.

column3:
City green space is absolutely essential to the health of community members. Loss of such space for the limited purpose of niche sports by individuals from outside the community is unacceptable. 

City green spaces are essential for public health, actively lowering mortality and reducing rates of cardiovascular disease, depression, and anxiety. These environments promote health by encouraging physical activity, restoring mental fatigue, fostering community social cohesion, and mitigating environmental hazards like air pollution and the urban heat island effect.
Comprehensive research from organizations like the U.S. EPA and the World Health Organization highlights three primary pathways through which green spaces benefit urban health:
1. Environmental MitigationAir & Noise Quality: Trees and vegetation absorb atmospheric pollutants and block traffic noise.Temperature Reduction: Parks combat the urban heat island effect, significantly reducing heat-related illnesses.
2. Mental Health & Cognitive RestorationStress Reduction: Immersion in nature lowers cortisol levels, blood pressure, and heart rate.
Mood Enhancement: Exposure to greenery boosts serotonin and dopamine, combating depression and attention fatigue.
3. Behavioral & Physical WellbeingIncreased Activity: Accessible trails, parks, and fields naturally promote exercise and reduce sedentary lifestyles.Social Connections: Shared communal spaces act as gathering hubs, which decreases loneliness and promotes community safety.

column6: This was never about pétanque for me. It is about the gap between public process and public awareness. The same gap is showing up in other neighborhoods and other cities, and it will keep happening here until we build the connective tissue that lets affected residents hear about decisions before those decisions are effectively made.  We have started a pilot Pol.is conversation at https://pol.is/2recpy3hxf for ongoing playground input. I would love to see it integrated with what Friends of Chimborazo Playground and the Church Hill Association are already doing, rather than become a new organization. The aim is a low-effort, moderated, inclusive channel that exists before there is a controversy.  And to the Boulefrogs: thank you for twenty years of involvement in the park. Nothing about the petition or the survey was a challenge to you. We are trying to widen the room, not push anyone out of it.
